primary_sources: Andrew Jackson, letter to Henry Lee, October 7, 1825

stimulus.text: “Mr. Adams is the Constitutional President and as such I would myself be the last man in the Commonwealth to oppose him upon any other ground than that of principle. How he reached the office is an enquiry for the succeeding canvass, when the principles of the Constitution, apart from his ministerial acts, or at least without necessary opposition to them, will sanction the investigation.” — Andrew Jackson, letter to Henry Lee, October 7, 1825.
stimulus.source_note: Andrew Jackson, letter to Henry Lee, October 7, 1825. Verbatim quotation; wording verified against the Library of Congress citation of the letter. Public domain.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: Jackson's letter best shows which change in American politics after the election of 1824?

options.text: The House of Representatives stopped choosing presidents
options.misconception: The House still held that power; Jackson is planning for the next election, not changing the Constitution.

options.text: A losing candidate could turn defeat into a popular campaign against elite deal-making
Henry Clay admitted that he had traded his votes for a cabinet office
options.misconception: Clay denied any bargain; Jackson is the one making the charge, and he offers no proof here.

options.text: John Quincy Adams resigned the presidency
options.misconception: Jackson calls Adams the Constitutional President; Adams served his full term.

rationales.A: The House kept its power to choose; Jackson looks to the next campaign instead.
rationales.B: Jackson accepts the result but saves the charge of a corrupt deal for “the succeeding canvass,” turning his loss into the theme of his 1828 campaign.
rationales.C: Clay denied the bargain; the charge is Jackson's, and this letter proves nothing.
rationales.D: Adams stayed in office; Jackson concedes he is the Constitutional President.
rationales.general:
1. Hear the two halves. Jackson calls Adams the Constitutional President, then says how Adams reached the office is a question for the next campaign.
2. Name the charge. Jackson's supporters said Adams won the House vote through a deal with Henry Clay, who then became secretary of state.
3. See the move. A loser who accepts the result but keeps the charge alive can run against the winners as a people's candidate.
Background: Jackson had won the most popular and electoral votes in 1824, yet the House chose Adams.
Remember: in mass politics, a defeat with a good story can be worth more than a win.
